cues.text: A Boy Fixed on the Blessed Sacrament
Born on January 31, 1673, at Montfort in Brittany, Louis-Marie Grignion — later known as Louis de Montfort — showed an unusual and consistent devotion to prayer from earliest childhood.
From the age of twelve onward, he visited the church both before and after his classes at the Jesuit college in Rennes without fail.
As a young man, he joined a society of fellow students who spent their free time ministering to the poor and incurably sick in local hospitals.
They read edifying books aloud to them during meals—an early, practical apprenticeship in the charitable and pastoral instincts that would define his priesthood.
An Itinerant, Controversial Preacher
Ordained a priest, Louis devoted himself to an intense itinerant preaching mission across western France’s rural parishes, particularly Brittany and the Vendée.
His missions drew large crowds but repeatedly aroused wary suspicion from local bishops and clergy, uneasy with his unconventional methods, uncompromising style, and popularity.
These tensions saw him removed from more than one assignment during his ministry and once, tradition holds, led opponents of his preaching to attempt to poison him.
Two Religious Foundations
Louis's missionary labors led him to found two religious communities intended to sustain and extend his work.

The Company of Mary (Montfort Missionaries) was a congregation of priests dedicated to continuing his preaching mission, while the Daughters of Wisdom was a community of women religious devoted to education and care of the sick and poor.
Both communities would grow substantially in the decades and centuries following his death.
The Daughters of Wisdom alone numbered some five thousand sisters across dozens of countries within two centuries.
A Manuscript Lost, Then Found
Near the end of his life, Louis composed a treatise on total spiritual consecration to Jesus through Mary.
He had preached this devotion tirelessly throughout his missionary career, summarized in the phrase totus tuus , "totally yours."
The manuscript, however, was set aside and essentially forgotten for over a century after his death.
It was rediscovered only by chance in 1842 at the motherhouse of his own religious community, and finally published the following year as True Devotion to the Blessed Virgin Mary .
A Pope's Motto

Once published, Louis's treatise gained an influence its author could scarcely have imagined during his own lifetime of controversy and repeated parish removals, becoming one of the most widely read works of Marian spirituality in the entire Catholic tradition.

Its central phrase, totus tuus , would be adopted centuries later as the personal papal motto of Pope John Paul II , who credited Louis's treatise with shaping his own understanding of Marian consecration from his youth onward.
Legacy
Louis died at Saint-Laurent-sur-Sèvre on April 28, 1716, worn out by the relentless pace of a missionary life that had never been widely comfortable within his own lifetime.
Beatified in 1888 and canonized in 1947, Louis de Montfort remains one of the great apostles of Marian devotion in Church history.

He was a controversial, sometimes embattled itinerant preacher whose forgotten manuscript, rediscovered by chance more than a century after his death, would significantly influence the Marian spirituality of Pope John Paul II.
